before: A class defines a reference type. An instance is one object created from that definition. new Counter() creates a new object each time it executes.
Score is a field: a named storage location inside each Counter object. public permits code outside the class to access it. The dot chooses a member of an object.
Assigning first to alias copies the reference, not the object. Updating alias.Score is visible through first. A separately created second object has its own field.
In these single-file examples, executable top-level statements come before class declarations. The class body defines members; it is not another sequence of top-level output instructions.
Expected behavior from this example: 6 then 0. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Create a third reference to second and change its Score; explain which names observe the change. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: A class defines a kind of object. Counter describes an object that can hold a score.
An instance is one object made from a class. Each new Counter() in this example creates a separate instance.
A field stores data inside an object. Each Counter has its own Score field, starting at zero. public lets the calling code access it, and a dot selects it.
Assigning first to alias copies a reference to the same object. It does not create another Counter. first and alias can both reach that object's score.
The program prints 6, then 0. Changing alias.Score changes the object shared with first. second is a separate object and keeps its own zero.
In this single-file program, the top-level steps come before the class definition. The class describes the objects; creating them happens when the new expressions run.

before.question: If alias.Score is assigned 9 instead, what do first.Score and second.Score print?
before.explanation: alias and first refer to the same object. second came from another new expression, so its initialized Score remains 0.

after.question: Set alias.Score to 9 instead. What do first.Score and second.Score print?
after.explanation: first shares the changed object with alias. second still has its separate score of zero.
